job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Olga Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Everyone I talk to is made up for this study, so there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the office by eight in Curitiba, in a room with six drafting desks and a kettle that's older than me. I'm a junior design engineer at a firm that plans small roads and drainage for towns. I draw the layouts in CAD, check the levels against the survey, and every second Thursday I go out to a site with a hard hat and a tape. I go home to a flat I share with two girls from my course, and my boyfriend, Tiago, comes over most nights.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me how you got into civil engineering and how you got this job.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My uncle laid pipes for the water company, and I liked watching the trenches. I did civil engineering at the federal university and got a good result, not a brilliant one. My final project was a small drainage plan for a flooding street in my neighbourhood, and I did one summer internship on a bridge repair. My mother sews uniforms from home, and she can't give me money, but she'd feed me for a month. I owe a little under nine thousand and have about seven weeks of costs saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good. I've been hearing about AI taking over for a few years and my office is still drawing the same roads. At work I'd say the tools save a minute here and there, and nobody I know has been replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not worried about the job itself. A road still needs somebody to walk it and look at the soil. But I'm worried about money, because junior pay doesn't go far, and the firm gets most of its work from the town councils, which are always short of funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep my head down. I'd stay in the shared flat, keep saving about a hundred a month, and push to do more site days, because I like them and nobody can do them from a desk. I still wouldn't use the AI tools. I don't trust a drawing I didn't check myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. Plain old worry about the rent and the councils, the kind that's always been there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the firm if the councils run out of money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we lose work and the first thing to go is the junior desk. There was a year when a firm down the road let four people go after a council changed its budget. I think about that more than I think about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not even try the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I once saw a colleague's drawing with a pipe that ran uphill, and the tool had put it there. He didn't catch it. I'd rather check everything slowly and know what I did. Maybe that makes me old before my time.

say: AI has been **talked about** for years and we still draw the same roads.
The tools save a **minute here and there**.
think: A road still needs somebody to **walk it** and look at the soil.
My worry is **council budgets** and junior pay that doesn't go far.
do: Ask for more **site days**, which nobody can do from a desk.
feel: **Fine**, with the old worry about rent and councils.
S0.quote: I think about that more than I think about robots.
fieldNote: Her real fear is **public budgets**, not machines.
Refusal of AI comes from a story: a pipe drawn **uphill** that nobody caught.
Plain, dry voice with short sentences.

steps.text: Ask the senior engineer for two extra site days a month
Save 100 pounds a month in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's getting serious, and our office should talk about it. If software starts doing the drawing and the checking, then what is a junior for? At work I'd say nothing much, because the boss hates complaints. To friends I'd say I'm watching it closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm uneasy and I'd say it's close to being afraid. A lot of my week is drawing standard layouts and checking numbers, which is what they say will go first. The firm has two juniors and one of us could be 'not replaced' when somebody leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay out of the software and double down on the things that are physical: the site visits, the soil tests, talking to the council engineer. I'd ask my boss if I could do a short course on surveying, because the survey work is outdoors. I'd also talk to Tiago about whether we move in together earlier to share costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Not panic, but the kind of feeling where you keep checking your phone for emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the survey course give you that drawing doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The surveyor goes to the place and measures it. A drawing is only as good as the numbers someone brings back. I think that person is harder to replace than the one who draws what they're given.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not learn the software tools to stay ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I should. But if the tools write the drawings, there are fewer jobs for people who use them. I'd rather be the one who stands on the ground. I know it sounds stubborn, and my sister says the same.

say: It's getting **serious**, and our office should talk about it, though the boss hates complaints.
I'd tell friends I'm **watching closely** and not much else.
think: Standard layouts and number checks are what goes **first**, and I'm one of two juniors.
A junior leaving might simply **not be replaced**.
do: Do more **site visits**, soil tests and council meetings.
Ask my boss to fund a short **surveying course**.
Discuss moving in with **Tiago** to share costs.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, the checking-my-phone kind of worry.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the one who stands on the ground. I know it sounds stubborn, and my sister says the same.
fieldNote: Her resistance is a **strategy**: be the person on the ground, not the desk.
Considers moving in with her boyfriend as a cost tactic, a small **family** step.
Admits her sister calls her stubborn.

steps.text: Ask the firm to pay for a short land surveying course
Move in with Tiago to share rent
Take on every site visit I can get

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and the government has to step in right away. At work I'd say it quietly to the senior engineer and ask what the firm plans. Online I wouldn't say much at all, because I think there's no point arguing, but I'd vote for anyone with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm very afraid for my job. The firm's whole business is the thinking work: planning, drawing, calculating. If AI can do that in two years, I don't see why they'd keep me. I'd have maybe three years before the robots take the site work, and that's not long enough to get far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every cost I can, give up the gym, and stop eating out. I'd go and look for a job with the water company my uncle worked for, because that's work in the ground that lasts longest. I'd ask my mother to let me move home if my job ends. Tiago and I would put off getting engaged, because it wouldn't feel right with money so uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. I'd lie awake adding up weeks of savings. I wouldn't tell Tiago the full number, because I don't want him worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you keep the number from Tiago?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he'd tell me it's fine and offer to cover me, and he earns baker's wages. I don't want to be a weight on him. But I know that's silly, and I'd probably tell him within a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Mum, I might lose the job, and I'm still going to be okay. She'd go quiet and then say she'd put aside some money from the uniform orders. I'd tell her not to. She'd do it anyway, in a biscuit tin.

say: It's **frightening**, and the government has to step in right away.
I'd quietly ask the senior engineer what the firm **plans**.
think: The firm's whole business is **thinking work**, so I don't see why they'd keep me.
Robots reach the site work in about **three years**, which isn't far enough.
do: Cut every cost, give up the **gym** and stop eating out.
Apply to the **water company** where my uncle worked.
feel: **Sick**, lying awake adding up my weeks of savings.
S2.quote: I'd say, Mum, I might lose the job, and I'm still going to be okay.
fieldNote: First scenario where she says out loud that she expects to **lose** the job.
Hides the real savings number from her partner, then admits she probably would not.
Looks to **utility work**, the one trade she knows from her uncle.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and stop eating out
Apply for trainee roles at the water company
Put off the engagement with Tiago for a year or two
Tell my mother I may move home if the job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning, and a sensible country would use it to retrain people. At work I'd say my piece to the boss and then see what the others think. Online I'd just vote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel a bit less afraid. By 2031 I'd be 27, with five years of site experience that most software can't copy. But I'd still be at risk when the thinking work goes, and I'd want to be somewhere that isn't so reliant on desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend two years getting as much field experience as I can and take the exam for a professional engineer's licence, which lets me sign off on work. I'd save more and aim for a year of costs by 2031. And I'd start learning the site-side digital tools like drone surveys, because they're hands-on, which I could live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not good, not terrible. Anxious but able to act, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a drone survey also a kind of technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I know I'm contradicting myself a little. But a drone is a tool I point at a place. A tool that writes my drawings makes my job smaller. Those feel different to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the licence change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A licensed engineer's name goes on the paperwork. If something goes wrong, there's a person to blame. I think firms will still want that person, even when the drawing itself is done by software.

say: Five years is a **decent warning**, and a sensible country would retrain people.
I'd say my piece to the boss and then **vote**.
think: By 2031 I'd have five years of **site experience** software can't copy.
I'd still be at risk when thinking work goes, so I want less **desk reliance**.
do: Build **field experience** and take the professional engineer's licence exam.
S3.quote: A drone is a tool I point at a place. A tool that writes my drawings makes my job smaller.
fieldNote: Sees a clear line between tools that **extend** her job and tools that shrink it.
Her **licence** plan rests on liability: a named person to blame.
Admits her own contradiction about drones, gently.

steps.text: Log site hours towards the professional engineer's licence exam
Save one year of living costs by 2031
Learn to run and process drone surveys on site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get through things sensibly. At work I'd say it's another change in an industry that always changes. To Tiago I'd say we could still plan our lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel safe enough for now and a bit wary later. I'd be 32, and probably senior with my own projects. I'd still keep some savings aside, because I've seen how fast a council's budget can fall through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the job, get my licence, and save for a small flat with Tiago. We might get engaged in two or three years and plan children for after that. I'd stay in the field and take on more site and client work as the desk work gets lighter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. I'd just feel normal, like a person who still has a normal life ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the long runway change your wedding plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it frees them. Tiago and I would plan for about three years from now, and my mother would be thrilled. In the two-year world I wouldn't even buy a dress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So where does the worry go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It goes small. It's the money for the flat and the council budgets, the same as today. I think having ten years makes the AI worry something I can plan around, not something that sits on my chest.

say: Ten years is **enough** to get through this sensibly.
It's another change in an industry that always **changes**.
think: I'd feel **safe enough** for now and a bit wary later.
I'd keep savings aside, because council budgets can **fall through**.
do: Carry on, get my **licence** and save for a flat with Tiago.
Plan an **engagement** in two or three years.
Take on more **site and client** work.
feel: **Pretty calm**, like a person with a normal life ahead.
S4.quote: Having ten years makes the AI worry something I can plan around, not something that sits on my chest.
fieldNote: Time converts fear into a **planning** problem.
The wedding is a good **marker** of how she feels in each scenario.
Still keeps a savings buffer from experience of council budgets.

steps.text: Pass the professional engineer's licence exam
Save for a small flat with Tiago
Plan the engagement and wedding for about three years ahead
Take on more client meetings and site leads

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by a long way. I'd have no time to build a skill or save enough, and the work I do is mostly thinking work for a few years. What would help is quick support for people like me, a firm that tells us early what it plans, and training that doesn't mean borrowing more.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say that not using AI doesn't mean not caring. I follow it closely, and I just prefer to understand what I put my name to. I'm someone who walks the site before drawing the road.

headlineQuote: I'm someone who walks the site before drawing the road.
portrait: Olga Santos is **22**, a junior design engineer at a small road and drainage firm in Curitiba.
She did civil engineering, owes under **nine thousand** and has seven weeks of costs saved, and shares a flat.
She's a centrist who prefers the familiar, takes few risks and **never uses AI tools**, after seeing a pipe drawn uphill.
Her moods run from uneasy to **alarmed** in the two-year world, where she'd look for utility work and delay her engagement.
Her plan is to be the person on the ground, through site work, a **licence** and surveying.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, since thinking work, the core of her firm, goes on a **short** timeline.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **support** for people like her, early honesty from the firm and training that doesn't add debt.
